name: Caldera Glyph
description: Caldera Glyph takes its name from the enormous volcanic calderas that pit its surface like the impressions of a stylus pressed into wax. Over forty major calderas have been mapped, each one kilometers across and hundreds of meters deep, their floors pooled with slowly cooling magma that hardens into patterns of dark basalt veined with brighter minerals. Between the calderas, vast plains of volcanic glass stretch to the horizon, their surfaces so smooth they reflect the tortured sky like dark mirrors.

The toxic atmosphere carries a constant rain of fine volcanic ash that accumulates on the glass plains in drifts that shift with the wind, creating an ever-changing calligraphy across the reflective surface. The exposed planetary core, visible at the intersection of three major calderas in the southern hemisphere, pulses with a deep orange light that fluctuates on a regular cycle—eleven hours of brightening followed by eleven hours of dimming, perfectly out of sync with the planet's rotation.

The temporal distortion zones are Caldera Glyph's most troubling feature. Localized pockets of spacetime that run at different rates from their surroundings have been confirmed in three locations, all near the glass plains. Equipment left in these zones ages decades in hours or, in some cases, appears to revert to earlier states. The mechanism is unknown, and the distortions do not correlate with any detected gravitational or electromagnetic anomaly. One theory links them to the planet's core fluctuation pattern.

Caldera Glyph has been classified as a hazard-zone world, with approach restricted to authorized research vessels only. The temporal distortions make any surface operation unpredictable and potentially dangerous, and two survey drones sent into the largest distortion zone returned with corrupted memory banks containing data timestamps from dates that have not yet occurred. Whatever process is writing and rewriting time on this world's glass surface, it operates by rules that remain wholly alien to current physics.
